newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russia, Ukraine trumpet new friendship.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Ukraine trumpet new friendship.

text.p: Russia and Ukraine trumpeted their new friendship on Saturday, sweeping painful issues under the carpet to achieve long-term stability between the two states.

Presidents Leonid Kuchma of Ukraine and Boris Yeltsin of Russia signed a long-delayed political accord ending a virtual "cold war" between the Slav former Soviet republics and committing them to a "strategic partnership".
Kuchma, who broke protocol to personally see Yeltsin off at Kiev's Boryspil airport, said he was strongly impressed by the results of the summit meeting.
"This was an event of huge importance which opens a new stage in relations between our two countries," Kuchma told reporters after Yeltsin's departure.
They signed a broad political declaration outlining views on domestic and international issues, documents hailing a deal on the Black Sea Fleet and a declaration on space cooperation.
Russia and Ukraine have been at odds over the shareout of the Fleet, Ukraine's energy debt, trade and other issues.
Moscow has jealously watched Kiev's drift towards the West while Kiev has suspected Moscow of reviving imperialism.
"Ukraine is a smaller country than Russia but there are fewer politicians in Russia now who think that Ukraine can be strangled by force and kept as a vassal," Kuchma said after Yeltsin's departure.

Kuchma and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin turned the tide on Wednesday when they agreed that Russia could lease Ukraine's Crimean port of Sevastopol to base its share of the fleet there for 20 years, solving the most painful problem.
Russia and Ukraine have also agreed that Moscow will pay for keeping Sevastopol by writing off part of a huge energy debt.
"We have no problems left. There are none," Yeltsin said after signing the treaty. But some big questions remained.
Officials on both sides differed strongly on details of the shareout of Sevastopol bays and about the debt, and it was not clear if parliaments would have to ratify the Sevastopol deal.
Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said in Kiev on Friday that the Kremlin leader had brought up Moscow's concerns about the rights of 12 million ethnic Russians in Ukraine.
He said Yeltsin was alarmed by reports of discrimination against Russian language and culture. Kiev denies there is any such thing.
Besides other outstanding issues, which include a tax union and delimitation of the border, both sides appeared keen to concentrate on long-term issues.
"The big treaty will not solve thousands of problems in relations between Russia and Ukraine," the analytical weekly Zerkalo Nedeli wrote. "But it will free hands to tackle them."
Each side was clearly looking towards the wider immediate benefits of concluding Saturday's deals.
"The main thing in the friendship treaty is that Moscow formally recognises Ukraine's independence, its territorial integrity," Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko told a news briefing on Saturday.

Moscow, which had failed to prevent NATO from granting membership to some of its former Warsaw pact allies in Eastern Europe, is now keen to stop the Western defence alliance moving further eastwards into the former Soviet republics.
Yeltsin signed a pact on special relations with NATO on Tuesday which gave Russia some say in the Western alliance.

Ukraine on Thursday initialled a deal guaranteeing it consultations with NATO if the need arose -- much easier for Moscow to swallow than Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia's commitment to seeking full membership.
